query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the stand-off distance from ~100 mm to ~70 mm and increasing the plasma/combustion power by 10–15% during thermal-spray deposition of the FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coat, while ensuring continuous inert gas shielding, will enhance in-flight particle kinetic energy and temperature, thereby improving splat flattening and inter-splat bonding to overcome the coating thickness shortfall relative to the 15–45 μm feedstock baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coat deposited using 15–45 μm powder under standard thermal-spray conditions (stand-off distance of ~100 mm, standard power settings, inert atmosphere) with a suboptimal thickness build-up.
generation.intervention: Optimize process parameters by reducing the stand-off distance to ~70 mm and increasing plasma/combustion power by 10–15%, with integration of real-time particle temperature and velocity sensors, all while maintaining an inert gas shield (e.g., Argon or Argon–H2 mixture).
generation.conditions: Deposition is performed in a controlled inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation, with the modified parameters applied during both the deposition process and initial coating build-up phase, ensuring that subsequent service under high-temperature cycling typical of TBC systems is not compromised.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced in-flight particle energy leads to more molten and better-flattened splats, resulting in increased inter-splat bonding and a higher deposition efficiency, which manifests as a thicker bond coat.
generation.mechanism: Increasing the particle temperature and velocity by reducing the stand-off distance and modestly increasing power improves the melting and impact dynamics of the HEA particles. This results in superior splat formation and dynamic interlocking with the substrate and pre-deposited layers, boosting overall coating thickness while the inert atmosphere suppresses oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coating thickness will be measurably higher than that achieved under baseline parameters, with maintained microstructural integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation. The improved deposition efficiency is expected to produce a bond coat that meets the thickness requirements without compromising high-temperature service performance.
generation.baseline: FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coat deposited with a feedstock of 15–45 μm under standard conditions (stand-off distance of ~100 mm and lower power settings), resulting in insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The intervention should remain within safe operational limits that prevent substrate overheating or coating microstructural degradation, and be effective under inert atmosphere deposition and subsequent high-temperature service conditions characteristic of thermal barrier coating systems.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the precise optimal combination of reduced stand-off distance and increased power to maximize thickness without triggering substrate damage or local oxidation. The real-time monitoring system is critical to mitigating this risk.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of thermal-spray depositions on FeCoNiCrAl bond coats with a systematic variation of stand-off distance (e.g., 70 mm vs. baseline 100 mm) and plasma power settings (baseline vs. +10–15%), while integrating real-time measurements for particle temperature and velocity to ensure process control. The coatings will be characterized for thickness buildup, microstructural integrity, and oxidation level.
measurements: Splat morphology and inter-splat bonding quality
In-flight particle temperature and velocity logs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating thickness does not increase significantly relative to the baseline, or if increased plasma power and reduced stand-off lead to excessive oxidation, substrate overheating, or degradation of coating microstructure (as evidenced by abnormal splat formation or microcracking), the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: As shown in Figure 9, the three-dimensional response surface model visually demonstrates parameter interactions. Analysis reveals that maintaining fixed laser power while elevating scanning velocity shortens the duration of laser–material interaction, consequently diminishing the molten zone’s liquid-phase volume. Meanwhile, a decrease in the powder feeding rate results in a reduced powder supply in the molten pool, ultimately leading to a smaller cladding area. When stabilizing scanning velocity, heightened laser power amplifies energy delivery per-unit time to the molten pool, enlarging its liquid-phase domain. Additionally, raising the powder supply rate enhances material input, further promoting the increase of the cladding area. Under consistent powder delivery conditions, enhanced laser power similarly elevates thermal energy input per-unit time, expanding the molten zone’s fluid state region. Notably, even with the prolonged laser interaction time caused by the reduced scanning velocity, larger cladding areas were achieved under these conditions. In this study, because of its appropriate particle size distribution and good flowability, the powder milled for 10 h was chosen as a feedstock to deposit a coating. Figure 8 shows the surface morphology of the APS AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating. From Figure 8a, it can be seen that the coating showed a rough morphology, which is usually observed on the surfaces of atmospheric plasma sprayed coatings []. It can be observed that at a higher magnification (Figure 8b), most of the splats were fully molten and well flattened, and the outlines of the flattened splats could be observed obviously. Some spherical and droplet-shaped particles with dimensions of less than 10 μm could also be found on the coating surface, which originated from the sputtering of the flying particles when impacting the already formed coating surface.

proposals.intervention: Adopt a bimodal feedstock powder distribution by supplementing the conventional 15–45 μm powder with a controlled fraction (e.g., 20–30% by weight) of coarser particles (45–70 μm)
proposals.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition in an inert (argon or argon–hydrogen) atmosphere with standard spray parameters, ensuring sufficient particle velocity and temperature; same substrate pre-treatment as baseline
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced deposition efficiency by larger, high-mass particles forming thicker, well-flattened splats with maintained microstructural homogeneity
proposals.mechanism: The coarser powder particles possess higher thermal mass and kinetic energy on impact, which promotes increased splat flattening and inter-splat bonding. They build up a thicker deposit per pass while the inert atmosphere maintains minimal oxidation during flight and deposition
proposals.predicted_outcome: An overall increase in coating thickness beyond the 15–45 μm feedstock baseline while preserving coating integrity, minimal oxidation, and proper bond coat adherence under both deposition and service conditions (elevated temperature cycling typical of TBC systems)
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It directly tackles the thickness shortfall by increasing the effective mass deposition rate without altering the alloy composition or compromising the oxidation control conditions, thereby ensuring the integrity of the as-sprayed coating

proposals.intervention: Optimize the thermal spray process by reducing the stand-off distance and increasing the plasma/combustion power to elevate particle in-flight kinetic energy
proposals.conditions: Conduct deposition under precisely controlled inert-gas shielding (argon or argon–H2) at a reduced stand-off distance (e.g., from 100 mm to ~70 mm) and a calibrated 10–15% increase in power settings, while monitoring particle temperature and velocity
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced in-flight particle heating and momentum transfer resulting in more impactful splats and a higher deposition efficiency leading to thicker builds
proposals.mechanism: Elevating the particle kinetic energy and temperature improves splat flattening and inter-particle bonding, increasing the effective deposition rate. At the same time, the inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation despite the increased energy input
proposals.predicted_outcome: A thicker bond coat relative to the baseline achieved without altering feedstock composition, with maintained oxidation levels and microstructural integrity under service conditions (thermal cycling and high-temperature exposure typical for TBC systems)
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It offers a single process parameter intervention that improves deposition efficiency and coating build-up, directly overcoming the thickness shortfall while adhering to oxidation control requirements

proposals.intervention: Integrate a localized, high-efficiency inert gas shield (nozzle or jet-based shrouding) at the spray gun exit to suppress oxygen entrainment during deposition
proposals.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition performed in an environment with an additional localized gas shroud supplying high-purity argon (or argon–H2 mixture) directly around the spray plume; maintain standard feedstock (15–45 μm) with adjusted nozzle geometry
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduced oxygen interaction at the particle flight and deposition stages preserving the native alloy surface; enhanced particle deposition yield due to minimized oxidation-induced splat disruption
proposals.mechanism: By confining the spray plume in a localized inert atmosphere immediately upon exit, the probability of oxidation is reduced, thereby preserving the high kinetic energy and reactivity of the particles that can then fuse more effectively into thicker deposits
proposals.predicted_outcome: A significant improvement in deposit thickness beyond the baseline while maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation and the overall coating microstructure, ensuring service reliability under high-temperature cycling
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It directly addresses the trade-off between deposit thickness and oxidation; the inert gas shrouding acts to preserve the pristine particle state during deposition, resulting in improved deposition yield and enabling a thicker bond coat

proposals.intervention: Preheat the substrate to an optimized elevated temperature to promote splat spreading and effective inter-splat bonding during deposition
proposals.conditions: Employ substrate preheating in the deposition chamber to temperatures up to 200–300°C (optimized below levels that would cause unwanted oxidation or phase changes) while maintaining standard inert atmosphere conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced splat flattening and increased bonding area at the interface, resulting in improved deposit cohesion and higher coating build-up rate
proposals.mechanism: Preheated substrates reduce the thermal gradient between the molten particles and the substrate, promoting better splat spreading and flattening. This higher degree of flattening increases the deposition efficiency and layer thickness, all while the inert gas environment limits oxidation
proposals.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in coating thickness relative to the baseline, with improved interfacial bonding and preserved as-sprayed oxidation levels, ensuring enhanced performance under both deposition and later high-temperature service in a TBC system
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It leverages thermal management of the substrate–particle interface to improve deposition efficiency without altering the feedstock or overall composition, directly addressing the thickness challenge while controlling oxidation

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention addresses the thickness shortfall by enhancing splat spreading and inter-splat bonding, which promotes increased deposition efficiency and build‐up.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraints by using substrate preheating within a controlled temperature window (200–300°C) to avoid unwanted oxidation or phase transformations, and it maintains an inert atmosphere.
critiques.physical_soundness: The physical mechanism is sound – reducing the thermal gradient improves splat flattening and bonding. However, care must be taken that the preheated substrate does not inadvertently promote substrate oxidation or undesired microstructural changes.
critiques.feasibility: Preheating the substrate is an established method in thermal spray processes and is technically feasible with existing deposition equipment.
critiques.evidence: While prior studies have demonstrated that substrate preheating can improve splashing behavior in thermal spraying, no specific records were provided to support this exact intervention for the FeCoNiCrAl system.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that even a moderate substrate preheat could locally increase oxidation rates or affect the microstructure if the temperature is not precisely controlled.
critiques.fix: Introduce a real-time substrate temperature monitoring system to ensure temperatures remain in the safe window and adjust preheat levels dynamically to avoid unintended oxidation.

critiques.constraints: It respects the process constraints by incorporating inert shielding and only applying a moderate increase (10–15%) in power and reducing stand-off distance, which should remain within safe operating limits.

decision.rationale: Direction D most directly targets the thickness shortfall by increasing in-flight particle energy through a controlled, moderate increase in plasma/combustion power and a reduction in stand-off distance. This intervention enhances particle heating and momentum transfer, promoting better splat formation and bonding without requiring changes to the feedstock. While there is a risk of overheating or substrate damage, this can be mitigated by integrating real-time particle temperature and velocity monitoring to fine-tune the power increase and stand-off distance, ensuring that the inert atmosphere still limits as-sprayed oxidation. Compared with other proposed interventions, D directly improves deposition efficiency while preserving coating integrity under the intended thermal barrier coating service conditions.
